Albany is a port city located in the Great Southern region of Western Australia. It is the oldest permanently settled city in Western Australia, predating Perth (state capital, situated 418 km SE) and Fremantle by more than two years. In June 2015, the estimated urban population of Albany was 33,970 making it state's 6th-largest population centre, with a total area of 297 km2 (115 mi2).

The city centre lies at the northern end of Princess Royal Harbour (part of King George Sound). Albany's business district is bounded by Mount Melville to the west and Mount Clarence to the east. The city is part of the local government area of Albany City.

Albany was established on December 26, 1826, as New South Wales' military outpost, which was part of a plan to prevent the ambitions of France in the region. On January 21, 1827 the outpost's commander, Major Edmund Lockyer, took possession of the continent's western third for the British Crown.

Initially, the area was named Frederick Town to honour the Duke of York and Albany, Prince Frederick. The settlement was transferred to control of Swan River Colony in 1831 and renamed Albany by Sir James Stirling (Lieutenant-Governor, 1791-1865).

During the last decade of 19th century, the city of Albany was served as a gateway to Eastern Goldfields. It was the only deep-water port of the colony for many years, having a place of prominence on shipping services between the Australian colonies and Britain. The opening of Fremantle Inner Harbour of 1897 saw its importance as port decline, and after that Albany's industries turned to agriculture, timber and whaling.

Nowadays Albany is a major tourist destination as well as a base from which to explore state's south-west. The city is well regarded for its preservation of heritage and natural beauty. 

Albany is a practical port for independent sightseeing. Most cruise ships berth at Berths 1 or 2, although some vessels may anchor and tender passengers to Albany Waterfront Marina. From the berth, passengers pass through the port’s Transit Shed before continuing by shuttle, taxi, tour vehicle or on foot.

Independent sightseeing: Easy in the town centre; transport or an organized excursion is recommended for the National Anzac Centre, Torndirrup National Park and the Historic Whaling Station.

Getting from the Cruise Port

  • Free port shuttle: Normally carries cruise passengers between the port and central Albany. Confirm the final return time before leaving the shuttle.
  • Walking: The town centre is approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) from the port, usually a 15–20-minute walk. Follow the flatter waterfront route along Princess Royal Drive and use the pedestrian overpass beside the Albany Entertainment Centre.
  • Taxis: A limited taxi collection point operates inside the port. Demand can be high when a large ship is visiting.
  • Private tours: Operators not contracted by the cruise line normally meet passengers in the public parking area outside the port, near the Albany Boatshed.
  • Tender calls: Passengers normally arrive at Albany Waterfront Marina, close to the waterfront but still separated from central York Street by the railway corridor.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore Central Albany and the Waterfront

Allow 2–4 hours. This is the easiest independent option. Start around York Street, where the Albany Visitor Centre, Town Hall, shops and cafés are concentrated, then walk downhill through the historic streets to the Museum of the Great Southern, the replica brig Amity and ANZAC Peace Park.

The waterfront is relatively level, but central Albany rises sharply away from the harbour. Passengers with limited mobility may prefer the shuttle for the journey between the port and York Street.

National Anzac Centre and Albany Heritage Park

Allow 3–4 hours. The National Anzac Centre stands within the Princess Royal Fortress on Mount Adelaide, approximately 3 km (1.9 mi) from central Albany. Its exhibitions, military sites and elevated views across King George Sound make it one of Albany’s most substantial attractions.

This visit is possible independently by taxi. A visitor-centre shuttle may operate on some cruise days, but it does not run continuously and should be confirmed after arrival. Walking from town involves sustained uphill sections and is unsuitable for passengers with limited time or mobility.

The Gap, Natural Bridge and Torndirrup National Park

Allow 3.5–5 hours. The Gap’s cantilevered viewing platform and the nearby Natural Bridge overlook the exposed Southern Ocean coast. The lookouts have constructed paths, but the national park is outside town and cannot be reached conveniently on foot or by regular urban sightseeing transport.

Organized excursion recommended. A prearranged tour or taxi is the practical choice, particularly if combining the park with additional coastal viewpoints. Conditions can be windy and wet, and visitors should remain on the designated paths. Park entry fees may apply.

Historic Whaling Station and the Southern Coast

Allow 4–5 hours. Albany’s Historic Whaling Station at Discovery Bay includes the former processing site, the restored whale chaser Cheynes IV, museum exhibits and a regional wildflower garden. It is well outside the walkable town area.

Choose a ship excursion, local tour or prearranged taxi. Longer tours sometimes combine the station with Torndirrup National Park, but check how much time is allowed at each stop.

Middleton Beach

Allow 2–3 hours. Binalup/Middleton Beach is approximately 3.2 km (2.0 mi) from central Albany and has a sheltered beach, lawns and views across King George Sound. A taxi is the simplest option for a short visit.

Walking is possible for active passengers, but the full return journey consumes considerable shore time and includes changes in elevation. Swimming conditions and local safety information should be checked on the day.

Self-Guided Albany Heritage Walk

Distance: Approximately 3 km (1.9 mi) from the central shuttle stop and back
Pure walking time: About 45–55 minutes
Recommended total time: 2–3 hours
Difficulty: Easy to moderate, with slopes between York Street and the waterfront

  1. Albany Visitor Centre and Town Square: Begin at the cruise-shuttle area near York Street and collect a current town map.
  2. York Street: Walk downhill through Albany’s main commercial street toward the harbour.
  3. Patrick Taylor Cottage: Detour into Duke Street to see one of Western Australia’s oldest surviving dwellings. Check locally before planning an interior visit.
  4. Stirling Terrace: Continue through the historic commercial precinct overlooking Princess Royal Harbour.
  5. Museum of the Great Southern: Explore the waterfront heritage precinct and its outdoor displays.
  6. Brig Amity: View the full-size replica sailing ship beside the museum precinct. Admission arrangements should be checked on arrival.
  7. ANZAC Peace Park: Follow the waterfront toward the memorial landscape at the foot of York Street.
  8. Albany Entertainment Centre: Continue along the harbour, then use the pedestrian connection to return uphill to York Street and the shuttle stop.

Passengers who walked from the ship can join the route near the Albany Entertainment Centre. For the return, allow additional time to reach the Transit Shed and complete port security procedures.

Practical Tips

  • Confirm whether your call is berthed or tendered, as the passenger arrival point will differ.
  • Albany’s weather can change quickly. Carry a light waterproof layer even when conditions appear settled.
  • Do not depend on finding an immediate taxi for a distant attraction; supply can be limited during large cruise calls.
  • Check the visitor centre for same-day transport to the National Anzac Centre and for any temporary trail closures in Albany Heritage Park.
  • For independent trips outside town, arrange the return journey in advance and keep a generous margin for traffic, tendering and port security.
